https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Russia's President Vladimir Putin tastes caviar as he visits Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu By Koh Ewe Published 13 August 2026, 05:46 BST Updated 1 hour ago Japan said it "strongly protests" against Vladimir Putin's visit to the Kuril islands on Thursday, the first time the Russian president had visited the disputed island chain. Russian state media reported that Putin visited Iturup - known in Japan as Etorofu - one of four islands in the Kuril chain that are claimed by Russia and Japan. Japan's foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi said the islands were "inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit". The countries have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. Four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. They are administered by Russia. At the end of World War Two, the Soviet Union annexed the island chain and deported around 17,000 Japanese residents. During his visit, Putin sampled fish roe and spoke to island locals, Russian state media reported. Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Japan has protested against previous visits by Russian officials to the disputed islands, including Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his predecessor Dmitry Medvedev. The Kuril islands are a strategic area for Russia, which has beefed up its military presence on the islands over the past decade. The island of Iturup is used as its primary military air base in the region. Last month, Chinese and Russian naval warships sailed through a strait in the Kuril islands during a joint patrol. Russia also holds regular military drills near the islands, drawing condemnation from Japan. Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/AP Catholicism ‘We live with a big burden’: US sexual abuse survivor hopes priest’s death brings closure Keith Townsend says he hopes death of Ronald Paquin in prison helps victims and families to ‘keep pressing forward’ Ramon Antonio Vargas Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a defrocked Boston Catholic priest who was portrayed admitting to molesting minors in the Oscar-winning Hollywood film Spotlight says he hopes the clergyman’s recent death in prison helps victims of his crimes and their families “keep pressing forward every single day”. “We live with a big burden in our hearts and on our backs,” Keith Townsend said on Wednesday while reflecting on the criminal charges which he successfully pursued against Ronald Paquin, who was imprisoned in 2019 and died in custody at age 83 on 11 September. “And my hope is that people can find closure and move on.” Those remarks by Townsend, 52, during a telephone interview were a notable reaction to the death of one of the key figures in the clergy sexual abuse and cover-up scandal with the Catholic archdiocese of Boston that – among other consequences – prompted the resignation of the institution’s archbishop, Bernard Law, at the end of 2002, as well as policy reforms across the US church. That same year, Paquin had pleaded guilty to sexually abusing an altar server from 1989 to 1992 while working at St John the Baptist church in the Boston suburb of Haverhill, Massachusetts . He was stripped of his clerical status and imprisoned in Massachusetts for that abuse, which was first publicly exposed in a Pulitzer-winning series of investigative articles by the Boston Globe newspaper’s Spotlight team. Paquin was freed in 2015. And learning of that release motivated Townsend – once a St John altar server, too – to come forward and report being abused himself by Paquin while on camping trips to Kennebunkport, Maine , between 1985 and 1989. View image in fullscreen Keith Townsend talks to the media outside court in Alfred, Maine in 2018. Photograph: Portland Press Herald/Getty Images As Townsend put it, he was between the ages of eight and 13 when Paquin molested him. Townsend recalled Paquin plying him with drugs and alcohol during the abuse, eventually leading him to battles with substance abuse addiction and incarceration. A Maine grand jury indicted Paquin in 2017 on new charges of gross sexual misconduct in connection with Townsend and another individual. Paquin faced a jury trial in November 2018 which culminated in a guilty verdict against him with regards to Townsend, though he was acquitted of having abused the other individual. Maine judge Wayne Douglas sentenced Paquin in May 2019 to 16 more years in prison. Paquin was in the Mountain View correctional facility in Charleston, Maine, when he died, the state’s department of correction said in a news release. Speaking five days later, Townsend said he first got word of Paquin’s death from his wife, who saw it circulating on the news and social media. He said he understood the many reactions which he subsequently heard or read that took delight in news of Paquin’s death. But Townsend, now a New Hampshire resident, also said he used the occasion to think about his “shaking off” the drug and alcohol addiction which had a grip on him in the wake of Paquin’s abuse. He said he contemplated the family he had built after overcoming “one of the biggest obstacles that could be thrown” at a person. “I get those who think the attitude should be, ‘Fuck him. Fuck what he did to me,’” Townsend said. “But look where I am today.” Townsend said he sought Paquin’s re-imprisonment with the aim of “protecting children … not [from] a man [but] a monster”. “Massachusetts just kind of let him go,” Townsend said. “So I had to dig deep … [because] I didn’t want anybody else to possibly have to go through [his] abuse. Maine thankfully had the balls to take this case, aggressively prosecute it and get a good outcome.” Townsend said he had not yet been able to see Spotlight, which dramatizes the Globe’s uncovering of the clergy sexual abuse scandal that roiled the city’s archdiocese. And therefore Townsend had not viewed the famous scene in the film in which Rachel McAdams , playing reporter Sacha Pfeiffer, confronts an actor portraying Paquin on his home’s front doorstep about allegations of molesting boys at St John the Baptist. “Sure, I fooled around – but I never felt gratified myself,” the actor playing Paquin, Richard O’Rourke, says in response as the journalist scribbles notes in a paper pad while wearing an astonished facial expression. “Right, um, but you admit to molesting boys at St John the Baptist?” McAdams’ Pfeiffer then asks O’Rourke’s Paquin. The latter’s reply: “Yes, yes. But, as I said, I never got any pleasure from it.” Another person closely familiar with Spotlight offered an opinion of that scene’s legacy on Wednesday. Attorney Mitchell Garabedian – who is portrayed in the 2015 movie by Stanley Tucci and has represented numerous victims of sexual abuse by Paquin and other clerics – said that part of Spotlight provided a powerful cue to survivors of clergy molesters that they were not alone. “It gave a sense of, ‘A-ha, I’m not the only one,’” in one of Hollywood’s most critically acclaimed films, Garabedian said. ‘“It wasn’t my fault, and I shouldn’t feel guilty.’” Townsend said ultimately he is grateful for anything that raised awareness about Paquin’s atrocities before his push to bring him to justice. “When I lay my head down tonight, I know it saved lives” getting Paquin imprisoned for his remaining years, Townsend added. “And that’s what matters to me.” Explore more on these topics Catholicism Boston US crime Spotlight Maine Rape and sexual assault Religion news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
